title: A Speedy Remedy That Isn't Speedy
hook: Habeas corpus lets a detained person ask a judge one question: is this lawful? The protection depends on getting an answer quickly — and ProPublica found some judges take months.
key_points: Habeas corpus is the procedure for asking a court to test whether someone's detention is lawful, and to order release if it isn't.
Its force comes from speed: a ruling that arrives after months of detention cannot give back the time already served.
ProPublica reports wide variation among federal judges in how long they take to decide habeas petitions from people held in immigration detention.
Because assignment is effectively a lottery, two people with similar claims can wait very different amounts of time for the same question to be answered.
Delay works one way here — the government's position is preserved by inaction, since the person stays detained while the petition sits.
The general lesson: for time-sensitive rights, how fast the process runs is part of the right, not a separate administrative detail.
content_html: Habeas corpus is one of the oldest protections against arbitrary imprisonment, and it is procedurally simple: a detained person asks a court whether their detention is lawful, and the court can order release if it is not. Almost all of its power lies in how fast that answer comes. A judge who eventually agrees you were unlawfully held cannot return the months you spent held.
extra_html: ProPublica's Carla Astudillo reported in September 2026 on how long federal judges take to rule on habeas petitions filed by people in immigration detention, finding wide variation — with some petitions sitting for months. Two features make that variation consequential. First, case assignment is effectively a lottery, so similar claims can receive very different waits. Second, delay is not neutral: while a petition is pending, the person remains detained, so inaction preserves the government's position by default. The transferable idea reaches well beyond immigration law — where a right is time-sensitive, the pace of the process is part of the right itself.

related.title: A Right With No Way to Sue Is Half a Right
related.hook: A prisoner's religious rights were violated and the harm was already done. The hard legal question was not whether it was wrong — it was whether he could recover anything at all.

related.title: A Time Limit Only Binds If Someone Counts the Clock
related.hook: A 72-hour cap on holding someone sounds like a hard limit. It is only as hard as the rule about when the count starts over.

related.title: Due Process
related.hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.

flashcards.prompt: What question does a habeas corpus petition put to a court?
flashcards.back_html: Whether the petitioner's detention is lawful — and if it isn't, the court can order their release.

flashcards.prompt: Why does the time a court takes to rule on a habeas petition matter so much?

choices.text: The remedy is release, so a late ruling cannot give back time already spent detained
Petitions are legally void if not decided within 30 days
Detainees are charged a daily fee while the petition is pending

flashcards.explanation_html: Habeas is a time-sensitive remedy. Speed isn't an administrative nicety here; it's most of what makes the protection real.

flashcards.prompt: In a pending habeas case, whose position does delay tend to favor?

choices.text: The government's — the person stays detained while the petition waits
The petitioner's — detention is suspended once a petition is filed
Neither; the case is frozen and the detainee released pending review

flashcards.explanation_html: Inaction preserves the status quo, and the status quo here is continued detention — which is why variation in judges' timelines has real stakes.
